title: Ofcom at an Inflection Point: Online Safety, Broadcasting and Telecoms
label: 20 October 2026 · Ofcom inquiry
summary: The Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee questioned Ofcom’s chair Sir Ian Cheshire and chief executive Dame Melanie Dawes about how the regulator is handling an expanded remit—especially online safety, AI harms, broadcasting impartiality, and telecoms infrastructure. Ofcom says it has transformed to meet new online risks, is pursuing stronger enforcement, and is asking Government for clearer tools and more resources; MPs pressed it on speed, legal limits to action, influence of big tech, and protection for vulnerable users.

glossary.definition: UK law giving Ofcom powers to require platforms to reduce harmful content and protect children online.
Technology and checks platforms use to verify a user's age to stop under-16s using social media.
A court-based power to disrupt an online service that causes serious harm; Ofcom says current measures are slow or limited.
Blocking access to a website or service for users in a specific country.
Rules about which services or news outlets appear most visibly on TVs, smart TV front pages or platforms.
Electronic Programme Guide — the TV menu listing channels and programmes.
A legal protection that shields platforms if they follow regulator codes, limiting the regulator's reach.
Video-sharing platform, like YouTube, which sits between traditional broadcasters and social media.

chapters.title: Ofcom’s expanded role and early assessment
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom has grown from a telecoms and broadcasting regulator into a multiregulator after taking on online safety; it has built capability but says new powers, resources and clearer tools are needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Sir Ian, this is your first appearance as Ofcom chair. What are your early impressions?

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: Ofcom is now a multiregulator. The addition of online safety was a big inflection point—450 staff were added and many codes written. We’re moving from rule-writing into enforcement and changing behaviour.

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: We’re respected and taken seriously internationally—big firms litigate against us—but we need to learn how to have faster, more impactful compliance work over the next three years.

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: The organisation has the synergies of covering both infrastructure and services—broadband, spectrum, data centres and platforms—but we do need to be clear when our legal tools fall short.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How will you show your primary duty to the public?

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: We will publish plans and metrics showing how we intend to 'move the dial' on harms, and review our structure and resources so the board can challenge the team to show impact.

chapters.title: Online safety: enforcement, limits and reforms
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom has opened many investigations and fines but says legal limits—especially on interim business disruption and extraterritorial enforcement—hamper fast action, so it’s asking Government for sharper tools and more resources.

turns.speaker: Dame Chi Onwurah
turns.text: Are Ofcom’s statutory duties to growth ever traded against protecting the public?

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: No. Our primary duty is citizens; growth duties are largely about infrastructure like fibre and spectrum. We won’t ignore harms to seek investment.

turns.speaker: Dame Chi Onwurah
turns.text: Can you make platforms adopt US safety changes voluntarily, especially for children?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: Some US voluntary commitments mirror our codes; others—like addiction—aren’t covered by the Act. The social media ban for under-16s will be the UK’s stronger tool.

turns.speaker: Mr Alaba
turns.text: Will Ofcom be ready to enforce the social media ban from day one?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: We’ve been preparing: we’ll publish an age-assurance report and consult on what 'highly effective' looks like. Platforms must implement age gates; enforcement will start when regulations are laid.

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: Expect gradual progress: technical fixes, platform relationships and cultural change. We shouldn’t promise instant, total removal of under-16s—circumvention is real.

turns.speaker: Liz Jarvis
turns.text: Why did the Grok AI nudification case take time and why no immediate business disruption?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: We opened enforcement quickly—faster than other regulators—but business disruption powers are clunky, the legal bar for urgent interim disruption is very high, and sometimes platforms self‑mitigate after public outcry.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: Many fines remain unpaid—what recourse do you have?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: We issued 11 fines: two paid, one under appeal, seven overdue. Some firms then adopted required safeguards or geo-blocked the UK. We pursue recovery, but extraterritorial limits can block full recovery.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: What legislative priorities would you press for?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: Top requests are: a faster, lower-bar interim business disruption process; powers to require proactive detection tech for illegal content; and clarification around safe harbour to shift more responsibility to platforms.

turns.speaker: Dame Chi Onwurah
turns.text: Are you asking for extra powers to deal with algorithmic harms, misinformation and AI-generated content?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: We are not asking now to widen the Act’s scope to cover all legal-but-harmful content, which is a political decision. But we will press for sharper enforcement tools and for YouTube/prominence work to be clarified.

chapters.title: Broadcasting standards and impartiality
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom defends its impartiality enforcement as consistent, but MPs pressed it over perceived bias on channels like GB News and whether rules are fit for modern opinion-led programming.

turns.speaker: Dr Rupa Huq
turns.text: People say Ofcom isn't doing enough about channels like GB News and TalkTV—are the impartiality rules being applied?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: We’ve opened many investigations into GB News and TalkTV; we apply 'due impartiality' after broadcast rather than pre-approving presenters. The rules don't demand strict equal time, but broadcasters must provide appropriate balance.

turns.speaker: Dr Rupa Huq
turns.text: Is there a double standard versus the BBC?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: The BBC has stricter internal rules for staff because of its public service role. Ofcom applies the Broadcasting Code consistently across licensed broadcasters.

turns.speaker: Liz Jarvis
turns.text: On Beverley Turner and other high-profile cases, why have investigations taken months?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: Investigations require evidence, information from broadcasters and legal checks; they can take time. In a recent GB News judicial review the court emphasised freedom of expression limits, so we've updated guidance accordingly.

turns.speaker: Jeff Smith
turns.text: Reality TV harmed contestants—will the broadcasting code be strengthened?

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: We’re waiting on Channel 4’s independent reports on 'Married at First Sight'. We’ve already been reviewing guidance for reality formats and will act quickly if rules need strengthening.

chapters.title: Prominence, media literacy and platform responsibilities
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom wants to protect public service news and help people navigate an algorithmic world, but prominence on platforms like YouTube raises hard questions about who counts as 'trusted' news and whether Ofcom or Parliament should set rules.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: What’s Ofcom doing on media literacy and prominence across broadcast and online?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: We’ve published guidance for platforms and broadcasters—flagging trusted content, user controls and better design—and call for prominence rules to be extended to smart TVs and, potentially, YouTube.

turns.speaker: Nigel Huddleston
turns.text: But who decides what is 'trusted news'? Is that a dangerous role for a regulator?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: That’s a big policy choice for Government and Parliament. Ofcom can implement a framework but we would want clear legislative principles if we were to be given that responsibility.

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: When young people get news from TikTok and YouTube, it becomes a national conversation about prominence and trust—but Ofcom should not unilaterally decide trustworthiness without Parliament.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you have the powers to regulate YouTube effectively?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: On media prominence, not fully; on safety and illegal content, yes under the Online Safety Act. That’s why prominence discussions in the Government’s Green Paper matter.

turns.speaker: Liz Jarvis
turns.text: Is the Online Information Advisory Committee helping?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: Yes—its independent expertise helps shape our approach to misinformation, crisis protocols and media literacy.

chapters.title: Telecoms, infrastructure and capacity to act
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom is working on telecoms transitions, 2G switch-off, coverage and spectrum, but warns that planning, local permission and legal limits affect service quality and enforcement outcomes.

turns.speaker: Dame Chi Onwurah
turns.text: Will the 2G switch-off harm vulnerable users as the fixed-line (PSTN) switch-off did?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: Operators have later schedules (2029–30) and there’s a voluntary concordat with Government to protect vulnerable customers; Ofcom's rules remain a backstop. But we can’t promise zero incidents—companies must identify and contact vulnerable users.

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: The industry learned from PSTN. The difference is better preparation now, but no system can guarantee absolutely no individual failures.

turns.speaker: Dame Chi Onwurah
turns.text: Are you improving how you measure 4G/5G service quality?

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: Yes—we’ve improved crowdsourced data on coverage and signal strength and published local analysis. Much local improvement depends on planning permission for masts; we’ve also enabled spectrum for high‑demand sites and satellite partnerships for remote areas.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you have enough resources and the right structure to move faster?

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: We have good capability but are asking for more resources for online safety. We’re reorganising enforcement—hiring a group director for enforcement—and using AI internally to speed consultations and processing.

turns.speaker: Dame Melanie Dawes
turns.text: We can be quicker and are cutting consultation timings by a quarter to a third, but implementing the social media ban and new telecoms tasks will need more people and budgets.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any closing point you wish we'd asked?

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: Please treat this as ongoing; we’ll return with details of our online safety review, specific resource asks and clearer outcome metrics to show impact and speed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final public comment: the teeth are there but the public wonders if the regulator has the stomach—how would you reply?

turns.speaker: Sir Ian Cheshire
turns.text: We have the stomach. We’re standing up enforcement and will push for legal fixes and resources to make action faster and more effective.
